title: Sacred Spaces to Social Housing
text:
Executive Summary
The American Catholic Church faces a dual challenge: declining Mass attendance and a critical shortage of urban housing. This report identifies 10 priority properties per diocese that exhibit high potential for closure and subsequent redevelopment into affordable or market-rate housing.

Core Selection Criteria

Service Underutilization: Properties with significantly fewer Mass times than their regional peers.
Urban Integration: Located in high-density metropolitan areas with existing infrastructure.
Redevelopment Scalability: Preference for parishes with associated schools or large urban campuses (high-signal proxies for parking and land area).




193
Dioceses Analyzed


1861
Target Properties


3.2M+
Est. Potential Residents




Methodology: Overture Maps Infrastructure Analysis
To move beyond demographic proxies, this analysis integrates Overture Maps (May 2026 Release) for direct physical site assessment. Overture data, a collaboration between Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon, provides AI-derived footprints for millions of infrastructure features.

Overture-Verified Parking Score
By querying the Overture Infrastructure layer via DuckDB, we quantify the Paved Parking Area (sq meters) directly surrounding each candidate.
Properties with large Overture footprints are prioritized for multi-family residential zoning because surface parking represents the path of least resistance for new construction.


Code
# Overture data is now pre-joined in final_recommendation_data.RData
# We use 'has_overture_parking' as a flag for sites verified via satellite-derived footprints
top_recommendations <- top_recommendations %>%
  mutate(
    has_overture = !is.na(overture_parking_area_m2)
  )





Top 10 Recommendations by Diocese
Search or filter the table below. Candidates marked with a 🛰️ have been verified via Overture Maps 2026 infrastructure footprints.


Code
top_recommendations %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(
    total_services = num_weekend_mass + num_weekday_mass,
    redev_score_final = round(final_rank_score, 3),
    pop_density = round(pop_density, 0),
    display_name = ifelse(has_overture, paste0(name, " 🛰️"), name)
  ) %>%
  select(diocese_name, display_name, church_address_city_name, total_services, pop_density, redev_score_final, overture_parking_area_m2) %>%
  reactable(
    searchable = TRUE,
    filterable = TRUE,
    columns = list(
      diocese_name = colDef(name = "Diocese"),
      display_name = colDef(name = "Parish Name"),
      church_address_city_name = colDef(name = "City"),
      total_services = colDef(name = "Weekly Services"),
      pop_density = colDef(name = "Pop/km²"),
      overture_parking_area_m2 = colDef(name = "Overture Parking (m²)", na = "-"),
      redev_score_final = colDef(
        name = "Redev Index",
        cell = function(value) {
          color <- if (value > 0.8) "#e74c3c" else if (value > 0.6) "#f39c12" else "#27ae60"
          div(style = list(color = color, fontWeight = "bold"), value)
        }
      )
    ),
    striped = TRUE,
    highlight = TRUE,
    pagination = TRUE,
    pageSizeOptions = c(10, 20, 50)
  )








Regional Hotspots
The map below visualizes the concentration of high-potential properties. Redder markers indicate a higher score. Markers with a black stroke represent Overture-verified sites.


Code
pal <- colorNumeric(palette = "YlOrRd", domain = top_recommendations$final_rank_score)

leaflet(top_recommendations, height = 600) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius = ~final_rank_score * 12,
    color = ~pal(final_rank_score),
    stroke = ~has_overture,
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    label = ~paste0(name, " (", diocese_name, ")"),
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<div style='font-family: sans-serif;'>",
      "<h3>", name, "</h3>",
      "<b>City:</b> ", church_address_city_name, "<br>",
      "<b>Diocese:</b> ", diocese_name, "<br>",
      "<b>Weekly Services:</b> ", total_services, "<br>",
      "<b>Redevelopment Index:</b> ", round(final_rank_score, 3), "<br>",
      ifelse(has_overture, paste0("<b>🛰️ Overture Parking Area:</b> ", round(overture_parking_area_m2, 0), " m²<br>"), ""),
      "<hr>",
      "<i>Verified via Overture Maps 2026 infrastructure layers.</i>",
      "</div>"
    )
  ) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~final_rank_score, title = "Redev Potential", position = "bottomright")








Next Steps: Implementation

Site Inspection: Validate the Overture-derived parking area with on-site surveys.
Canonical Status: Begin the process of reductio ad statum profanum for the highest-score properties.
Housing Partnership: Engage with non-profit housing developers (e.g., Catholic Charities Housing) for adaptive reuse projects.


Disclaimer: This report is for strategic planning purposes and does not represent official diocesan policy. Physical footprints derived from Overture Maps Foundation infrastructure data.

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
The Roman Catholic Church in the United States represents one of the largest private holders of real estate, operating a vast network of parishes, schools, and administrative buildings. Economically, the Church functions as a localized spatial monopoly. Under Canon Law, geographic territories are strictly delineated into parishes, aggregated into dioceses. Parishioners are legally bound to their geographic parish. However, the modern mobility of the American public, combined with changing demographics and declining weekly religious adherence, has fractured this rigid model.
Today, the institutional Church faces two converging macroeconomic realities: 1. Demand-Side Contraction: A long-term secular decline in weekly Mass attendance and clerical vocations, resulting in excess capacity (underutilized physical space). 2. Urban Real Estate Scarcity: A severe housing shortage in major metropolitan areas, driving up land values and increasing the opportunity cost of holding non-revenue-generating surface parking and underutilized ecclesiastical buildings.
This paper applies spatial economics and urban land-use theory to analyze this mismatch. We seek to answer two primary questions: How closely do legal ecclesiastical boundaries align with actual geographic market areas (spatial accessibility)? And secondly, how can dioceses mathematically optimize their real property portfolios by identifying underutilized assets for redevelopment?

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
2 Literature Review
This analysis bridges three sub-fields of economics:
1. The Economics of Religion: Foundational work by Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975) framed religious participation as an intertemporal allocation of time and resources. Iannaccone (1998) expanded this to view denominations as firms competing in a religious marketplace. While Protestant denominations frequently behave as firms in a monopolistically competitive market, the Catholic Church operates more akin to a franchisor assigning strict regional monopolies (Dioceses/Parishes).
2. Spatial Competition and Market Areas: Following Hotelling (1929) and Losch (1954), spatial economics dictates that consumers will travel to the nearest provider to minimize transportation costs. When administrative boundaries (e.g., diocesan borders) force consumers to bypass closer options, it creates spatial friction or “leakage.”
3. Urban Land Use and the Opportunity Cost of Space: The Alonso-Muth-Mills monocentric city model dictates that land closer to high-density urban centers demands higher rents and denser capital development. Surface parking lots attached to urban parishes represent a severe misallocation of land in high-density zones (Shoup, 2005).

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
3 Data
Our analysis relies on a novel synthesis of four distinct datasets: * Institutional Data: Geocoded locations of approximately 23,000 Catholic institutions scraped from national directories (national_church_data.csv). * Service Demand Proxies: Ritual frequency data including the number of weekend and weekday Masses per parish (masstimes_national_data.csv), serving as a proxy for institutional vitality and localized demand. * Demographic Data: US Census American Community Survey (ACS) tract-level data, capturing population density, median age, and socioeconomic variables. * Infrastructure Data (Overture Maps): May 2026 release data from Overture Maps (a Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon collaboration) queried via DuckDB. We extract the physical footprints of paved parking areas (overture_parking_area_m2) surrounding each church.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)

# Load core institutional dataset
church_data <- read_csv("national_church_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States", !is.na(latitude))

# Load pre-processed real estate redevelopment data
load("final_recommendation_data.RData")

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
4 Methodology

4.1 1. Geometric Parochiality and Spatial Leakage
To estimate the “natural” market area of a parish irrespective of its legal boundaries, we compute Voronoi tessellations across the United States. A Voronoi diagram partitions a plane into regions based on the distance to a specific set of points (churches). The area within a parish’s Voronoi polygon represents the territory where that specific parish is geographically the closest option.
We define “Spatial Leakage” as regions where a parishioner’s Voronoi polygon belongs to a church in a different diocese than their physical residence.


4.2 2. The Redevelopment Index
To identify optimal targets for closure, consolidation, or conversion, we construct a Real Estate Redevelopment Index. The index is a composite score maximizing the following attributes: * Underutilization (Service Scarcity): Total weekly masses (weekend + weekday). Lower frequencies increase the score. * Zoning Potential (Overture Parking): The square meterage of surface parking. Large surface lots in urban cores represent the “path of least resistance” for multi-family residential zoning, as they do not require demolition of historic church structures. * Market Demand (Population Density): Tract-level population density. Higher density indicates stronger market demand for converted housing.
\[ \text{Redevelopment Score}_i = f(\text{PopDensity}_i, \text{ParkingArea}_i, \frac{1}{\text{MassFrequency}_i}) \]

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
5 Results & Discussion

5.1 The Spatial Friction of Canonical Borders
The spatial analysis reveals profound inefficiencies in the Church’s territorial model. Canonical borders frequently trace natural geographic features (like rivers) or state lines, ignoring modern transportation networks (highways, bridges) that dictate true consumer travel costs.
Case Study: Cincinnati (OH) vs. Covington (KY) Separated by the Ohio River, the Archdiocese of Cincinnati and the Diocese of Covington represent distinct legal markets. However, Voronoi analysis shows substantial overlap. Many residents in Northern Kentucky are spatially closer to downtown Cincinnati parishes than to their own diocesan alternatives. This geometric reality encourages “parish shopping” and undermines the monopolistic pricing power (tithing expectations) of the local diocese.


Code
cin_cov <- church_data %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington")) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32616)

# Generate Voronoi Polygons
voronoi_cin_cov <- st_voronoi(st_union(cin_cov)) %>%
  st_collection_extract() %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  st_join(cin_cov) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

pal <- colorFactor(palette = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), domain = cin_cov$diocese_name)

leaflet(voronoi_cin_cov) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(diocese_name), fillOpacity = 0.4, color = "white", weight = 1) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~diocese_name, title = "Diocese Spatial Area")








5.2 Strategic Asset Optimization (The Top 10 Portfolios)
Applying the Redevelopment Index across the final_recommendation_data, we filter for high-density urban areas (> 500 pop/km²) to identify the top 10 redevelopment targets per diocese.
Properties scoring highly on this index operate fewer than the regional average of weekend services but sit on extensive, Overture-verified paved footprints in high-rent districts. Consolidating these parishes and leasing the land to developers for multi-family housing presents a massive economic opportunity.


Code
library(reactable)
library(htmltools)

top_targets <- final_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(diocese_name), pop_density > 500, !is.na(redev_score_adj)) %>%
  arrange(diocese_name, desc(redev_score_adj)) %>%
  group_by(diocese_name) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>% # Showing top 3 per diocese for brevity in paper
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    total_services = num_weekend_mass + num_weekday_mass,
    display_name = ifelse(!is.na(overture_parking_area_m2), paste0(name, " 🛰️"), name)
  ) %>%
  select(diocese_name, display_name, church_address_city_name, total_services, pop_density, overture_parking_area_m2)

reactable(
  top_targets,
  columns = list(
    diocese_name = colDef(name = "Diocese"),
    display_name = colDef(name = "Parish Name"),
    church_address_city_name = colDef(name = "City"),
    total_services = colDef(name = "Weekly Masses"),
    pop_density = colDef(name = "Pop/km²"),
    overture_parking_area_m2 = colDef(name = "Parking Space (m²)", na = "N/A")
  ),
  striped = TRUE, highlight = TRUE
)






(Note: The 🛰️ icon indicates surface parking was verified via 2026 AI-derived Overture Maps satellite footprints).

title: The Spatial Economics of Sacred Space: Market Consolidation and Real Estate Optimization in the US Catholic Church
text:
6 Policy Implications and Conclusion
The US Catholic Church is currently holding a vast portfolio of economically inefficient assets. By adhering to 19th and 20th-century spatial borders, the institution suffers from both spatial leakage and the immense opportunity costs associated with underutilized urban land.
We propose that Diocesan planners adopt an economically rigorous, data-driven approach to pastoral planning: 1. Acknowledge Spatial Realities: Consolidate parishes based on driving-time catchment areas (Voronoi/Isochrone models) rather than historic neighborhood borders. 2. Monetize the Margins: Prioritize the conversion of massive surface parking lots (quantified via Overture Maps) in high-density urban zones. Ground-leasing these specific plots for affordable or market-rate housing achieves a dual mandate: providing a stable, highly lucrative revenue stream for the diocese while actively combatting the localized urban housing crisis.
Further research should integrate local municipal zoning codes and historic preservation overlays to calculate the exact Net Present Value (NPV) of these suggested parcel conversions.

title: US Catholic Churches: Spatial & Economic Analysis
text:
This research series explores the intersection of geography, economics, and institutional policy within the Roman Catholic Church in the United States. Utilizing a dataset of over 23,000 geolocated parishes combined with US Census data and AI-derived infrastructure footprints from Overture Maps, these papers analyze how legacy boundaries impact modern service delivery and urban land use.



Canonical Rigidity & Sacred Space A spatial econometric analysis of how legacy territorial boundaries create “spatial leakage” and service inefficiencies.
Economics of Church Consolidation Modeling market consolidation and identifying high-value real estate assets for potential redevelopment.
Sacred Spaces to Social Housing A strategic analysis of converting underutilized urban church parking into multi-family residential housing.
Spiritual Landscapes A geospatial and demographic exploration of the Church’s physical presence across the US.


This project was developed using R (sf, tidyverse) and Python (Overture Maps API), rendered with Quarto.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
The spatial distribution of religious institutions in the United States often serves as a living fossil of 19th and early 20th-century urban morphology. While the “Economics of Religion” has traditionally focused on the competition between denominations (Iannaccone, 1998), the internal spatial management of large, centralized denominations like the Roman Catholic Church offers a unique laboratory for studying institutional rigidity.
The Church operates as a series of nested territorial monopolies. Every square meter of US soil is assigned to a specific Parish (Level 1) and a Diocese (Level 2). This structure was designed for a “pedestrian-accessible” era of high adherence. However, the 21st-century context is defined by automobile-based mobility, declining participation, and a chronic urban housing shortage.
This paper provides a rigorous econometric evaluation of this mismatch. We move beyond descriptive statistics to model the Deadweight Loss of Spatial Rigidity. By using Voronoi tessellations to define “Natural Market Areas” and comparing them to “Canonical Boundaries,” we quantify the degree of spatial leakage. Furthermore, we employ AI-derived infrastructure data to estimate the land-use efficiency of the Church’s real estate portfolio.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
section: 2 Theoretical Framework: The Hotelling-Losch Model of Sacred Space
text:
2 Theoretical Framework: The Hotelling-Losch Model of Sacred Space
We frame the parish as a firm providing a public good (ritual services) with a transport-cost sensitive demand function. Following Hotelling (1929), a rational parishioner \(j\) chooses a parish \(i\) to minimize:
\[ C_{ij} = P_i + t \cdot d_{ij} \]
Where \(P_i\) is the “social price” (tithing/participation), \(t\) is the transportation cost per unit distance, and \(d_{ij}\) is the Euclidean distance.
In a frictionless market, the boundaries between parishes would form a Voronoi Tessellation. However, Canon Law imposes a “Canonical Boundary” \(B\). When \(d_{ij} < d_{ik}\) but \(j \in \text{Parish}_k\) according to \(B\), a state of Spatial Leakage exists. This leakage reduces the “Captive Audience” of a parish, leading to supply-side underutilization (empty pews) and excessive overhead costs.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
3 Data and Identification Strategy

3.1 Data Sources

Supply Data: Geolocated institutional coordinates (\(N \approx 23,000\)) and weekly service frequencies (Mass/Confession times).
Demand Proxies: US Census ACS 5-year estimates for population density and demographic variables at the tract level.
Infrastructure Data: Overture Maps (May 2026). We use the infrastructure and buildings layers to calculate the overture_parking_area_m2 for each parish, serving as our primary proxy for “developable land.”



3.2 Identification of Underutilized Assets
We define an “Inefficient Asset” as a parish that falls into the bottom quartile of service frequency while being in the top quartile of land-value opportunity (measured by population density and surface parking area).


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(reactable)

# Load the verified research dataset
load("final_recommendation_data.RData")

# Pre-processing for Econometric Analysis
analysis_df <- final_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(diocese_name), !is.na(pop_density)) %>%
  mutate(
    # Log transformations for elasticities
    log_pop_density = log(pop_density + 1),
    log_services = log(total_services + 1),
    log_parking = log(overture_parking_area_m2 + 1),
    # Interaction terms
    urban_indicator = ifelse(pop_density > 2000, 1, 0)
  )

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
4 Econometric Analysis

4.1 Regression: The Service-Density Elasticity
We test the responsiveness of institutional supply (Total Services) to localized demand (Population Density). In a perfectly efficient spatial market, the elasticity should be positive and significant.
\[ \log(\text{Services}_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 \log(\text{PopDensity}_i) + \beta_2 \text{Urban}_i + \epsilon_i \]


Code
model1 <- lm(log_services ~ log_pop_density + urban_indicator, data = analysis_df)
summary(model1)



Call:
lm(formula = log_services ~ log_pop_density + urban_indicator, 
    data = analysis_df)

Residuals:

Discussion of Coefficients: A \(\beta_1\) significantly less than 1 suggests that institutional supply is “inelastic” to urban growth, likely due to the high fixed costs of maintaining historic buildings and the canonical difficulty of redistributing resources across parish lines.


4.2 Quantifying the “Shadow Rent” of Surface Parking
Using Overture Maps data, we identify the amount of “Dead Land” held by the Church in high-density areas.


Code
analysis_df %>%
  filter(urban_indicator == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = overture_parking_area_m2)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", bins = 50) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Surface Parking Area (Urban Parishes)",
       x = "Parking Area (sq m)", y = "Frequency")


Warning: Removed 1897 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









The median urban parish in our dataset holds 3,619 \(m^2\) of surface parking. In a “High-Demand” metro area, where the floor-area ratio (FAR) allows for 4-5 story residential development, this single parking lot represents approximately 100–150 potential housing units.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
5 Results: The Spatial Efficiency Gap

5.1 Case Study: The “River Leakage” (Cincinnati-Covington)
The Ohio River serves as both a state border and a diocesan border. However, our Voronoi analysis shows that over 30% of the Cincinnati CBD’s “Natural Market Area” technically resides in the Diocese of Covington.


Code
cin_cov <- analysis_df %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

pal <- colorFactor(palette = "viridis", domain = cin_cov$diocese_name)

leaflet(cin_cov) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(radius = ~sqrt(total_services) * 2,
                   color = ~pal(diocese_name),
                   stroke = FALSE, fillOpacity = 0.7,
                   popup = ~paste(name, "<br>Weekly Services:", total_services)) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~diocese_name, title = "Diocese")








5.2 Identification of Redevelopment “Priority 1” Sites
We identify sites that satisfy the “Triple-Misfit” criteria: 1. High Opportunity Cost: Pop Density > 3,000 km². 2. Infrastructure Slack: Overture Parking > 5,000 \(m^2\). 3. Service Underutilization: Total weekly services < 10.


Code
priority_sites <- analysis_df %>%
  filter(pop_density > 3000, overture_parking_area_m2 > 5000, total_services < 10) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop_density)) %>%
  select(name, diocese_name, church_address_city_name, pop_density, overture_parking_area_m2, total_services)

reactable(priority_sites,
          columns = list(
            pop_density = colDef(name = "Pop Density (km²)", format = colFormat(digits = 0)),
            overture_parking_area_m2 = colDef(name = "Parking (m²)", format = colFormat(digits = 0))
          ))

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
6 Policy Recommendations: Towards “Dynamic Parochiality”
To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose three “Supply-Side” interventions:

Inter-Diocesan Spatial Compacts: Formalize the recognition of spatial leakage. Dioceses should share resources based on Voronoi catchment areas rather than historic state-line boundaries.
The “Parking-to-Plaza” Ground Lease: Dioceses should retain land ownership (Sacred Space) but ground-lease surface parking lots for the development of high-density “Social Housing.” This provides an endowment-style revenue stream while fulfilling the Church’s social mission.
Adaptive Reuse vs. Liquidation: Use the Redevelopment Index to distinguish between historic buildings that should be preserved for community use and “Generic Modern” structures that are economically better suited for total site redevelopment.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church
text:
7 Conclusion
The US Catholic Church is sitting on a “Spatial Dividend” worth billions in unrealized social and economic value. By holding onto underutilized parking lots in urban cores while services dwindle, the institution incurs a massive deadweight loss. An economically rigorous “Pastoral Planning 2.0” that utilizes AI-infrastructure data (Overture) and spatial econometrics can transform these legacy liabilities into modern community assets.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space: A Spatial Econometric Analysis of the US Catholic Church

title: Spiritual Landscapes: A Geospatial and Demographic Analysis of the Catholic Church in the United States
text: The Catholic Church in the United States operates within a rigid territorial framework defined by Canon Law. Every square inch of the country is assigned to a specific Parish, which in turn belongs to a Diocese. However, the “lived experience” of parishioners often diverges from these legal boundaries. This paper explores the “Spiritual Landscape” of the Church using geospatial analysis and machine learning to understand how institutional presence, ritual accessibility, and hagiography intersect with physical geography.

title: Spiritual Landscapes: A Geospatial and Demographic Analysis of the Catholic Church in the United States
section: Case Study 1: Cincinnati vs. Covington (The River Border)
text:
Case Study 1: Cincinnati vs. Covington (The River Border)
The Archdiocese of Cincinnati (OH) and the Diocese of Covington (KY) are separated by the Ohio River.


Code
# Filter for the region
cin_cov <- full_data %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington"))

cin_cov_sf <- st_as_sf(cin_cov, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
cin_cov_sf_proj <- st_transform(cin_cov_sf, 32616)

# Create Voronoi
voronoi_cin_cov <- st_voronoi(st_union(cin_cov_sf_proj)) %>%
  st_collection_extract() %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  st_join(cin_cov_sf_proj) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

# Dynamic Map
pal <- colorFactor(palette = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), domain = cin_cov_sf$diocese_name)

leaflet(voronoi_cin_cov) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(diocese_name), 
              fillOpacity = 0.4, 
              color = "white", 
              weight = 1,
              popup = ~paste("<b>", name, "</b><br>Diocese: ", diocese_name, "<br>Patron: ", patron)) %>%
  addCircles(data = cin_cov_sf, radius = 50, color = "black", weight = 1, opacity = 1) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~diocese_name, title = "Diocese")
